parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قامره (kamara, “(legislative) chamber”), ultimately from Latin camera (“deliberative body”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قامبور (whence modern Turkish kambur), of Greek origin.

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كناره (känarä, “edge, margin”), from Classical Persian کناره (kanāra, “edge, side”). Compare кена́р (kenár) from Ottoman Turkish كنار (känar, “edge, margin”) from Classical Persian کنار (kanār, “edge, side”).

parole.significato: gaff; boat-hook; setting pole; pike pole
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قانجه (kanca), from Venetan ganzo.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قین (kın).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قنطار (kantar). Doublet of це́нтнер (céntner).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish, from Arabic قَنْطُورِيُون (qanṭūriyūn), from Ancient Greek κενταύρειον (kentaúreion). Cognate with English centaury.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قپاق (kapak) (Turkish kapak), from verb قاپامق (kapamak).

parole.significato: kapama (traditional Southwestern Bulgarian dish made with sauerkraut, rice, various meats (pork, veal, black pudding, s…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قپامه (kapama, “an act of shutting, closing, confining; a kind of coat or cloak closing in front; a kind of stew, prepared in a closed vessel”), from قپامق (ḳapamaḳ, “to close, to shut, to confine”).

parole.significato: door, gate (typically with a roof above)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قاپو (kapı, “door”).

parole.significato: a type of traditional knife; also identified with a yataghan
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish (dialectal) قرهقولاق (kara-kulak, “a type of weapon”), calqued from Classical Persian سیاهگوش (siyāh-gōš, literally “black ear”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قرنفل (karanfil), from Arabic قَرَنْفُل (qaranful).

parole.significato: cinereous vulture (a Eurasian black vulture, Aegypius monachus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قرتال (“booted eagle”)..
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قسوت (qasavet) (whence modern Turkish kasvet), from Arabic قَسْوَة (qaswa).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قصاب (kassâb), borrowed from Arabic قَصَّاب (qaṣṣāb).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قصاب (kassâb). By surface analysis, каса́п (kasáp) + -ин (-in).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قات (kat).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قطران (katran), from Arabic قَطْرَان (qaṭrān).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قهوهجی (ḳahveci). By surface analysis, кафе́ (kafé) + -джия (-džija).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قفس (kafes).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قهوهخانه (kahvehane).

parole.significato: kaftan (tunic, historically worn by the upper class in Middle Eastern societies)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قفتان (kaftan), from Classical Persian خفتان (xaftān).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قاچاماق or قاچامق (ḳaçamaḳ, “escapade”). Cognate with Albanian kaçamaku and Greek κατσαμάκι (katsamáki).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كباب (kebap), from Arabic كَبَاب (kabāb); see there for more.

Ostensibly French quelle f (“which, what”, feminine of quel m) + файда́ f (fajdá, “benefit, use”), literally “what use”. Файда́ (Fajdá), in turn, is from Ottoman Turkish فایده (fayda), Ottoman Turkish فائده (fa'ide).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كیسه (kese), from Classical Persian کیسه (kīsa), ultimately from Akkadian 𒋢𒃻𒉌𒌓 (kīsu, “leather bag for weights and silver; silver capital; treasury”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كستانه (kestane) (Turkish kestane) or German Kastanie, from Ancient Greek κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كهربار (kehribar, kehrübar), vulgar form of كهربا (kehrüba), from Classical Persian کهربا (kahrubā).

parole.significato: a particle used for emphasis, insistence, or emotional coloring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كه (ki), borrowed from Classical Persian کِه (ki).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كبریت (Turkish kibrit)), from Arabic كِبْرِيت (kibrīt).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كلار (kiler), from Byzantine Greek κελλάριν (kellárin), from Koine Greek κελλάριον (kellárion), from Latin cellārium.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كلیم (kilim), from Classical Persian گلیم (gilīm), from Ancient Greek κάλυμμα (kálumma, “covering”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كرپیچ (kerpiç, kirpiç).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قبور (“quiver”) (whence modern Turkish kubur).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوجه (koca).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوز (koz, “trump”).

Simplified from an earlier карчи́чек (karčíček), borrowed from dialectal Ottoman Turkish كارچیچیك (karçiçek, “snow flower”). Possibly influenced by Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “speck, grain”), whence dialectal Bulgarian коки́чка (kokíčka, “kernel”).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قولاك (kolañ, “girth, girdle, belt”). Compare Romanian colan (“girdle”), Macedonian колан (kolan, “belt”), Serbo-Croatian колан (“girth”); other Turkish borrowings. Stefan Mladenov's proposal of Italian origin is only true for Romanian colan (“necklace”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قمار (kumar), from Arabic قِمَار (qimār).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قمارجی (kumarcı) (compare Turkish kumarcı); equivalent to кома́р (komár, “gambling game, hazard”) + -джия (-džija).
Per the Bulgarian Etymological Dictionary, possibly from dialectal Ottoman Turkish [script needed] (kombulak, “oak gall”), with regressive assimilation: u - a > a - a.

In the form кана́п (kanáp) and partially semantically borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قنب (kınnap), from Arabic قِنَّب (qinnab, “hemp”), else inherited Old Church Slavonic конопь (konopĭ), from Proto-Slavic *konopь.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوپچه (kopça).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوص قوجه (kos koca), whence Turkish koskoca, an emphatic form of koca. See Turkish koskocaman for another example of such an emphatic construction.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوغه (kova).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوچ (koç, “ram”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قله (kulle).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خمبره (kumbara).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوندورا (kundura) (whence modern Turkish kundura /kondura).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قورشون (kurşun).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كسور (küsûr), from Arabic كُسُور (kusūr). Compare Serbo-Croatian кусур (“change, money given back”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قصور (kusur), from Arabic قُصُور (quṣūr).

parole.significato: box, case (container with a flat base and sides)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوطی (kutu, kutı) (extended with the suffix -ия (-ija)), ultimately from Greek κουτί (koutí).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوتسز (kutsız, “unlucky”). Oftentimes, wrongly written as **куцу́с (**kucús) because of its phonetic and semantic resemblance to native Bulgarian куц (kuc, “limping”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قوشاق (whence modern Turkish kuşak).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قنا (kına), from Arabic حِنَّاء (ḥinnāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قیرمه (kırma).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قسمت (kısmet), from Arabic قِسْمَة (qisma).

parole.significato: haunch, croupe (rear body part) of an equine or another tetrapod
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قیچ (whence modern Turkish kıç (“back, butt”)).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كومور (kömür), from Proto-Turkic *kömür (“coal”), akin with Turkish kömür, Macedonian ќумур (ḱumur).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كوفته (köfte), from Classical Persian کوفْتَه (kōfta, “kofta”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كار (kâr, “profit”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لاله (lale), from Classical Persian لاله (lāla).

parole.significato: old-fashioned cataplasm (usually made of flour or barn mixed with water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لاپا (lapa). Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish [Term?] (“lapa”). Cognate with Greek λαπᾶς (lapᾶs), dialectal Albanian lapë, Romanian lapă, Aromanian lapa with similar meanings.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لگن (leğen), from Classical Persian لگن (lagan), ultimately from Ancient Greek λεκᾰ́νη (lekắnē).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لوفر (lüfer), from Greek λουφάρι (loufári). Compare Turkish lüfer and Russian луфарь (lufarʹ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لاش (leş), from Classical Persian لاش (lāš).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لوقوم (lokum), from a vulgar form of Ottoman Turkish راحت الحلقوم (râhatü'l-hulkûm), from Arabic رَاحَة الْحُلْقُوم (rāḥat al-ḥulqūm).

parole.significato: Warm southerly wind that blows during spring; souther. Specifically, wind blowing from the Aegean Sea (from the south w…
parole.testo: From лодо́с (lodós), apparently by devoicing of the д (d) to a т (t). That term originally from Ottoman Turkish لودوس (lodos), from Byzantine Greek νότος (nótos).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لوله (lüle), from Classical Persian لوله (lūla).

Derived from Ottoman Turkish لیلاق (leylak). The expected outcome is principally лилак (lilak) (attested dialectally), but in Bulgarian it has been reanalyzed under the influence of native люлея (ljuleja, “to rock”), люлка (ljulka, “swing”).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish معدنوس (mağdanos, maydanos), from Arabic معدونس (maʕdūnis), from Byzantine Greek μακεδονήσιον (makedonḗsion, “parsley”). See the Ottoman Turkish entry for cognates in other languages.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مزراق (whence modern Turkish mızrak), of Arabic origin. Medial -д- between ж and р is epenthetic.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مغازه (mağâza).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish میمون (meymûn / maymun), from Arabic مَيْمُون (maymūn). The computing sense derives from the symbol's visual resemblance to a monkey curled up or hanging by its prehensile tail.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مالاق (malak, “buffalo calf”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مانغال (mangal), from Arabic مِنْقَل (minqal).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مانجه (manca), from Italian mangia. First attested in 1843.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish محرمه (whence Turkish mahrama), from Arabic مَحْرَمة (maḥrama, “kerchief”).
Borrowed from a dialectal variant of Ottoman Turkish مارپیچ, from Classical Persian مارپیچ.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مصرف (masraf), from Arabic مَصْرَف (maṣraf).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ماسره (masra), from Arabic مَاسُورَة (māsūra). The spelling is probably influenced by that of масра́ф (masráf) or is a misspelling of масра́ (masrá).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ماسوره (“duct, tube”) (whence modern Turkish masura), of Arabic origin.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish محله (mahalle), borrowed from Arabic مَحَلَّة (maḥalla). Cognate with Romanian mahala.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish میدان (meydan), from Arabic مَيْدَان (maydān).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مزه (meze), from Classical Persian مزه (maza, “taste, snack”).

parole.significato: field that is free to be used for pasture
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مرعی / مرعا (merʼa) (whence Turkish mera (“grassland”)), from Arabic مَرْعًى (marʕan).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish میخانه (meyhane).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مناره (Turkish minare), from Arabic مَنَارَة (manāra).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مور (mor).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مسقی (musakka), from Arabic مُسَقَّعَة (musaqqaʕa), from the trilateral root ص ق ع (ṣ q ʕ): “to hit, to pound, to smash”. Cognates include Greek μουσακάς (mousakás), Romanian musaca and Serbo-Croatian musàka /муса̀ка.

parole.significato: oilskin, oilcloth (watertight covering, especially a tablecloth which does not need to laundered)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مشمع (muşamma), from Arabic مُشَمَّع (mušammaʕ, “waxed; covering dipped in wax”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مشمله (muşmula), from Greek μούσμουλο (moúsmoulo).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مؤذن (müezzin) (Turkish müezzin), from Arabic مُؤَذِّن (muʔaḏḏin). Compare Serbo-Croatian мујезин/mujezin.

parole.significato: clog, patten (footwear with a rigid sole)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish نعلین (nalın) (whence modern Turkish nalın), of Arabic origin.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish نار (nâr), from Classical Persian نار (nār).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish نخود (nohut), from Classical Persian نخود (naxōd).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish نفت (neft), from Classical Persian نفت (naft).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish نشان (nişan), from Persian نشان (nešân, “sign, signal, target”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish اوطه (“chamber”). Doublet of ватог (vatog).
Derived from йо́ргован (jórgovan).

From Ottoman Turkish عثمان (osman) (the Ottoman Empire in Bulgarian, османска империя (osmanska imperija) is referred to after its founder, Osman I), hence cognate with Macedonian османски (osmanski), Serbo-Croatian отомански, English Ottoman, and with many other European equivalents. Doublet of ото
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پادشاه (pâdişâh), from Classical Persian پادشاه (pādišāh, “monarch”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پازار (pazar), from Classical Persian بازار (bāzār).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پلانقه (palanka).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پاموق (pamuk).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پانجار (pancar, “beetroot”), from Armenian բանջար (banǰar, “edible greens, vegetable”), from Old Armenian բանջար (banǰar, “edible greens, vegetable”).

parole.significato: para (the smallest Turkish coin, worth ¹⁄₄₀ of a kuruş)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پاره (pare, para), from Classical Persian پاره (pāra).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پرتل (partal, “worn-out cloth”), a -lı derivative of Classical Persian پارچه (pārča, “piece, part”). Displaced Bulgarian пъртищ (părtišt), which is cognate with the Persian lemma.
From Ottoman Turkish پارچه (parça).

parole.significato: pastirma, pastrami (highly seasoned, air-dried cured beef)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish باصدرمه (pastırma).

parole.significato: eggplant, aubergine (vegetable of species Solanum melongena)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پاتلجان (patlıcan), from Classical Persian بادلجان (bādiljān), ultimately of Dravidian origin.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish; equivalent to Modern Turkish patırdı (extended with the hyperbolic suffix -ия (-ija)).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پاچه (paça), from Classical Persian پاچه (pāča). Cognate with Albanian paça, Greek πατσάς (patsás), Romanian pacea.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پاچاوره (paçavra).

parole.significato: pasha (title in the Ottoman Empire or its holder)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پاشا (pāšā).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پیغامبر (peygamber), from Classical Persian پیغامبر (payġāmbar).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پیكه (peyke), from Classical Persian پایگاه (pāygāh).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پرده (perde), from Classical Persian پرده (parda).

parole.significato: lower end, edge, brim of cloth or apron
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پش (peş, “back”), from Classical Persian [Term?].
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پیشكیر (peşkir), from Classical Persian پیشگیر (pēšgīr).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پشتمال (peştemal, peştamal, peştimal), پیشتمال (piştemal), from Classical Persian پشتمال (puštmāl), from پشت (pušt, “back, rear of the body”) + مال (māl, “cleaning”). Other cognates include Albanian peshtamall, Aromanian pishtamal and Serbo-Croatian пештѐма̄љ /peštèmālj

parole.significato: pilaf (a dish made by browning grain, typically rice, in oil and then cooking it with a seasoned broth, to which meat a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پلاو (pilav), from Classical Persian پلاو (pilāw), from Hindustani पुलाव (pulāv) / پُلاؤ (pulāo), from Sanskrit पुलाक (pulāka, “lump of boiled rice”).

parole.significato: heather (evergreen shrub or small bush of genus Erica)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پيرين (piren) (obsolete or dialectal within the modern language?).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پیچ (piç), from a dialectal form of Armenian բիճ (bič), from Middle Armenian բիճ (bič).

Colloquialized reflex of Ottoman Turkish پيستول (“pistol”) (itself a French or German borrowing), ultimately of Slavic origin. By surface analysis, пищя́ (pištjá, “to squeak, to scream”) + -ов (-ov). Also borrowed into Romanian pișcol (colloquial), Greek πιστόλι (pistóli)).

parole.significato: poturs (type of slacks worn by the upper class in the Ottoman Empire)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پوتور (potur) (whence modern Turkish potur) + native plural marker. Ultimately of Armenian origin.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پرانقه (pranga, “fetters”). For some of the semantics, see also *prǫga (“linkage”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پشت (püşt), from Classical Persian پشت (pušt, “rear side, back”), which, together with Sanskrit पृष्ठ (pṛṣṭha, “back, hinder part”), is akin to Proto-Slavic *pьrstъ.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish راقی (rakı).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish راف (raf), from Arabic رَفّ (raff).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish روغنی (revğani), in turn from Classical Persian روغن (rawġan, “oil, butter”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish رزنه (rezene), from Classical Persian رازیانه (rāziyāna).

parole.significato: grater for food preparation; mandoline (kitchen cutter)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish رنده (rende), from Classical Persian رنده (randa).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish رشوت (rüşvet), from Arabic رُشْوَة (rušwa, “bribe”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صایوانت (sayvant, “awning, canopy; fringe”), from Classical Persian سایبان.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ساقسی (saksı).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صالقم (salkım, “cluster, bunch of grapes”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صومون (somun).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صندوق (sandık).

parole.significato: saddler, leatherworker (a person who makes or repairs saddles, harnesses, and other leather equipment for horses)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سراج (saraç), from Arabic سَرَّاج (sarrāj).

parole.significato: dolma, sarma (stuffed cabbage or grape leaves)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صرمه (sarma).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سودا (sevda), from Arabic سَوْدَاء (sawdāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صدف (sedef), from Arabic صَدَف (ṣadaf).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سدف (sedef), from Classical Persian سداب (sadāb).

parole.significato: prostration, the movement during Islamic prayer
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سجده (secde), from Arabic سجدة (“prostration”).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سایسخانه (seyishane). It went through two sound changes: metathesis of /s/ and /h/, then a sound change /h/ > /k/. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian сехсана, Serbo-Croatian сексана and Serbo-Croatian сејксана, etc.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سلوی (selvi, “cypress”).

parole.significato: stall (bench or table on which small articles of merchandise are exposed for sale)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سركی (sergi).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سیكدیر (sikdir).

Per the Bulgarian Etymological Dictionary, the word is likely a blending of several words with different etymologies: * from ясми́н (jasmín) with a loss of the initial я- (ja-), consistent with a dialectal meaning of "wild jasmine"; * from Ottoman Turkish سیمین (simin, “silvery, silver”) from Classi
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صوی (compare Turkish soy).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صوپه (sopa) (whence modern Turkish sopa).

parole.significato: sujuk, a type of dry, spicy sausage usually in the shape of a horseshoe, common in Bulgaria and other Balkan countries
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صوجوق (sucuk).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سلطان (sultan), from Arabic سُلْطَان (sulṭān).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سلطنت, from Arabic سَلْطَنَة (salṭana). By surface analysis, султа́н (sultán) + -ат (-at).

parole.significato: a foal of a mule that has never been saddled
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صپا (sıpa).

parole.significato: sea sponge (asymetric basal animal of family Spongiidae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سونگر (süñger, “sponge”) (whence Turkish sünger), a reflex of Byzantine Greek σφουγγάριον (sphoungárion). Distantly akin to native Bulgarian гъ́ба (gắba, “fungus”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تاوه (tava), from Classical Persian تاوه (tāwa).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تاوان (tavan).

parole.significato: bug-a-boo, bogey, hobgoblin; apparition (evil nocturnal spirit that frightens people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish [script needed] (tılısım, tılsım, “talisman; magic, sorcery; ghost, apparition”), from Arabic طَلَاسِم (ṭalāsim) - plural of طِلَسْم (ṭilasm, “enigma; talisman”), from Ancient Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, “talisman; sanctified object”). Cognate with Macedonian таласам (talas
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طپه (tapa).

parole.significato: tarator (a cold summer soup, usually consisting of yoghurt, oil, water and various vegetables such as cucumber and garl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تراتور (tarator).

parole.significato: An unceremonious, cunning and impudent man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طریقت (tarikat), from Arabic طَرِيقَة (ṭarīqa, “path, road”).

parole.significato: wire (used in purely mechanical applications of metal thread)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تل.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تگلتی (teğelti).

parole.significato: pot, saucepan (A deep, covered cooking vessel with two side handles.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تنجره (tencere, “saucepan, cooking pot”), from Arabic طَنْجَرَة (ṭanjara).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تپه (“summit, top”). Identical with modern Turkish tepe.

parole.significato: knitted or woven footwear (similar to slippers)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ترلك (terlik) (whence modern Turkish terlik).

parole.significato: stubborn, unreasonable, difficult, impossible to deal with
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ترسنه, cognate to Modern Turkish tersine.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish دسته (deste, teste), from Classical Persian دسته (dasta, “handle, huft”) (interpreted as an nt-stem).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish دفتر (defter), borrowed from Arabic دَفْتَر (daftar, “register; notebook”).

parole.significato: kind of Ottoman Empire fief granted by the Sultan to a spahi (спахи́я (spahíja)) in exchange for his cavalryman service…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تیمار (timar).

parole.significato: buckle, clasp (metal clasp used for fastening two things together, such as the ends of a belt, or for retaining the end…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طوقه (toka).

parole.significato: large wooden rod for pestle, used in conjunction with a large mortar of stone called дибе́к (dibék)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طوقماق (tokmak).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طوپ (top, “ball, clump”).
